claim: Each saccade shifts the projections of the visual scene on the retina.
source: Each saccade shifts the projections of the visual scene on the retina.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the effects of eye movements on retinal projections.

claim: Receptive fields of neurons in oculomotor areas are predictively remapped to account for retinal shifts during saccades.
source: It has been proposed that the receptive fields of neurons in oculomotor areas are predictively remapped to account for these shifts.
evidence: This is a proposal cited from the literature about neural mechanisms.

claim: Selection by attention may limit remapping processes to a subset of attended locations.
source: While remapping of the whole visual scene seems prohibitively complex, selection by attention may limit these processes to a subset of attended locations.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on inference about computational complexity.

claim: Attentional selection consumes time.
source: Because attentional selection consumes time, remapping of attended locations should evolve in time, too.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the temporal dynamics of attention.

claim: Remapping of attended locations should evolve in time.
source: Because attentional selection consumes time, remapping of attended locations should evolve in time, too.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the temporal properties of attention.

claim: No remapping of attention was observed when the cue appeared shortly before saccade.
source: We observed no remapping of attention when the cue appeared shortly before saccade.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: When the cue appeared sufficiently early before saccade, attentional resources were reallocated precisely to the remapped location.
source: In contrast, when the cue appeared sufficiently early before saccade, attentional resources were reallocated precisely to the remapped location.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Pre-saccadic remapping takes time to develop.
source: Our results show that pre-saccadic remapping takes time to develop suggesting that it relies on the spatial and temporal dynamics of spatial attention.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing timing-dependent effects.

claim: Pre-saccadic remapping relies on the spatial and temporal dynamics of spatial attention.
source: Our results show that pre-saccadic remapping takes time to develop suggesting that it relies on the spatial and temporal dynamics of spatial attention.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The visual system compensates for retinal shifts using a copy of the motor command.
source: It has been proposed that the visual system compensates for such shifts using a copy of the motor command (Sperry, 1950) to anticipate changes in the visual scene from the planned eye movement.
evidence: This is a proposal from the literature, supported by citation to Sperry, 1950.

claim: We typically do not keep track of the whole visual scene.
source: However, we typically do not keep track of the whole visual scene (O'Regan et al., 1999; Rensink et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to O'Regan et al., 1999 and Rensink et al., 1997.

claim: Visual compensation could be restricted to salient or task-relevant objects selected by spatial attention.
source: Studies have proposed that such visual compensation could be restricted to salient or task-relevant objects, selected by spatial attention (Cavanagh et al., 2010; Rolfs and Szinte, 2016).
evidence: This is a proposal from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Behavioral compensation could result in anticipatory deployment of spatial attention to the retinal location that a visual stimulus will occupy after the saccade.
source: At the behavioral level, this compensation could result in anticipatory deployment of spatial attention to the retinal location that a visual stimulus will occupy after the saccade (Jonikaitis and Theeuwes, 2013; Rolfs et al., 2011; Szinte et al., 2015; Szinte et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Attention is allocated at a spatial target location almost immediately after a saccade.
source: Such anticipatory deployment could explain observations that attention is allocated at a spatial target location almost immediately after a saccade (Jonikaitis et al., 2013; Yao et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jonikaitis et al., 2013 and Yao et al., 2016b.

claim: Remapping triggers an anticipatory and sometimes pre-saccadic response of neurons in FEF, LIP and SC with receptive fields centered on the post-saccadic retinal location of the attended object.
source: Remapping triggers an anticipatory and, sometimes, pre-saccadic response of neurons in frontal eye fields (FEF), lateral intra-parietal area (LIP) and superior colliculus (SC) with receptive fields centered on the post-saccadic retinal location of the attended object (Duhamel et al., 1992; Sommer and Wurtz, 2006; Walker et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neurophysiology studies.

claim: Remapping can facilitate tracking of task-relevant objects across saccades and allow rapid comparison between pre- and post-saccadic visual inputs.
source: Remapping can facilitate tracking of task-relevant objects across saccades and allow rapid comparison between pre- and post-saccadic visual inputs (Crapse and Sommer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crapse and Sommer, 2012.

claim: The remapping hypothesis has been challenged with new data collected within the FEF.
source: However, this remapping hypothesis has been challenged with new data collected within the FEF (Chen et al., 2018; Zirnsak and Moore, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2018 and Zirnsak and Moore, 2014.

claim: Before a saccade, neurons respond to stimuli presented near the saccade target rather than to stimuli presented at remapped locations of the recorded receptive field.
source: These studies found that, before a saccade, neurons respond to stimuli presented near the saccade target rather than to stimuli presented at remapped locations of the recorded receptive field (RF).
evidence: This refers to findings from Chen et al., 2018 and Zirnsak and Moore, 2014.

claim: Convergent remapping is towards the saccade target in dissociation of forward remapping which would be parallel to the saccade vector.
source: These results were later termed 'convergent remapping' towards the saccade target in dissociation of the 'forward remapping', which would be parallel to the saccade vector (Neupane et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is terminology and conceptual framework from Neupane et al., 2016a.

claim: Convergent remapping could manifest behaviorally as a spatially unspecific spread of attention around the saccade target.
source: They led to the proposal that convergent remapping could manifest behaviorally as a spatially unspecific spread of attention around the saccade target (Zirnsak and Moore, 2014).
evidence: This is a proposal from Zirnsak and Moore, 2014.

claim: Remapping of spatial attention before saccades could be reinterpreted as attentional spread between saccade target and remapped location.
source: Remapping of spatial attention before saccades, as reported in behavioral studies, therefore could be reinterpreted as attentional spread between saccade target and remapped location (Jonikaitis et al., 2013; Rolfs et al., 2011; Szinte et al., 2015; Szinte et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a reinterpretation of previous behavioral findings in light of convergent remapping.

claim: Convergent remapping effects predict that locations surrounding the saccade target by up to 10 degrees of visual angle would receive all attentional benefits before the eyes start to move.
source: Such interpretation of the convergent remapping effects predicts that locations surrounding the saccade target by up to 10 degrees of visual angle (dva) would receive all attentional benefits before the eyes start to move.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the convergent remapping hypothesis.

claim: There are no behavioral studies mapping pre-saccadic attention in sufficient detail to disambiguate whether attention converges towards the saccade target or is remapped in parallel to the saccade target.
source: To date, there are no behavioral studies mapping pre-saccadic attention in sufficient detail to disambiguate whether attention converges towards the saccade target, or is remapped in parallel to the saccade target, as earlier behavioral work suggested.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the literature at the time of writing.

claim: Attention was allocated to the saccade target location and did not spread to nearby positions about 4.2 degrees of visual angle apart.
source: We observed that attention was allocated to the saccade target location and did not spread to the nearby positions, about 4.2 degrees of visual angle (dva apart.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: If remapping is an attentional process, it will take some time for the attention shift to occur.
source: Our reasoning was that if remapping is an attentional process (Cavanagh et al., 2010; Rolfs and Szinte, 2016), it will take some time for the attention shift to occur (Ling and Carrasco, 2006; Müller and Rabbitt, 1989; Nakayama and Mackeben, 1989; Rolfs and Carrasco, 2012).
evidence: This is reasoning based on cited literature about attention dynamics.

claim: Stimuli presented just before a saccade would not leave enough time for remapping to develop and to be observed before the saccade.
source: Therefore, stimuli presented just before a saccade would not leave enough time for remapping to develop and to be observed before the saccade.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the temporal dynamics of attention.

claim: Stimuli presented early enough should be remapped before the saccade.
source: On the other hand, stimuli presented early enough should be remapped before the saccade.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the temporal dynamics of attention.

claim: When the cue appeared shortly before saccade onset, spatial attention was allocated at the cued location but not at its remapped location.
source: Indeed, we found that when the cue appeared shortly before saccade onset, spatial attention was allocated at the cued location but not at its remapped location.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: When the cue appeared sufficiently early before saccade onset, attentional resources that were initially drawn to the cued location were re-allocated to its remapped location.
source: In contrast, when the cue appeared sufficiently early before saccade onset, attentional resources that were initially drawn to the cued location were re-allocated to its remapped location (i.e. the retinal location it will occupy after the saccade).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: To achieve comparable discrimination at different eccentricities, the discrimination target had to be tilted by 4.42 ± 0.86° if presented at the fixation target.
source: We observed that to achieve comparable discrimination at different eccentricities, the discrimination target had to be tilted by 4.42 ± 0.86 ° (mean ± SEM), if presented at the fixation target.
evidence: This is a measurement from the threshold task.

claim: The discrimination target tilt gradually increased with eccentricity, finally reaching 14.10 ± 1.40° at eccentricities between ~15.3 and ~16.2 dva.
source: This tilt gradually increased with eccentricity, finally reaching 14.10 ± 1.40 ° at eccentricities between ~15.3 and~16.2 dva (see Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a measurement from the threshold task, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Saccade latency was longer when the visual streams overlapped with the fixation and saccade targets (217.56 ± 3.77 ms) compared with when they didn't overlap (186.00 ± 2.61 ms, p < 0.0001).
source: Saccade latency was longer when the visual streams overlapped with the fixation and saccade targets (217.56 ± 3.77 ms) compared with when they didn't overlap (186.00 ± 2.61 ms, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The difference in saccade latency resulted from the saccade target and fixation being less visible if they overlapped with the visual streams.
source: This indicates that such difference resulted from the saccade target and fixation being less visible if they overlapped with the visual streams.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the saccade latency data.

claim: Presentation of the discrimination target did not disrupt saccade preparation.
source: Altogether, these results show that presentation of the discrimination target did not disrupt saccade preparation, demonstrating that the stimuli we used to measure the allocation of attention did not directly interfere with its deployment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the saccade latency and accuracy analyses.

claim: On trials without a cue, increased visual sensitivity (0.88 ± 0.05) was found at the saccade target location relative to the average of all other tested positions (0.42 ± 0.04, p < 0.0001).
source: On trials without a cue (Figure 2A–C), we found increased visual sensitivity (0.88 ± 0.05, normalized d' and SEM, respectively) at the saccade target location relative to the average of all other tested positions (0.42 ± 0.04, p < 0.0001, Figure 2B), suggesting that attention shifted towards the saccade targets during saccade preparation.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Attention shifted towards the saccade targets during saccade preparation.
source: On trials without a cue (Figure 2A–C), we found increased visual sensitivity (0.88 ± 0.05, normalized d' and SEM, respectively) at the saccade target location relative to the average of all other tested positions (0.42 ± 0.04, p < 0.0001, Figure 2B), suggesting that attention shifted towards the saccade targets during saccade preparation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the visual sensitivity data.

claim: Attention at the saccade target did not spread to the surrounding positions (0.40 ± 0.04, p < 0.0001).
source: Attention at the saccade target clearly did not spread to the surrounding positions (0.40 ± 0.04, p < 0.0001 , Figure 2C), with sensitivity benefits being constrained to the immediate vicinity of the saccade target.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data comparing saccade target to surrounding positions.

claim: No deployment of spatial attention to the fixation target (0.41 ± 0.05) was observed compared with the average across all other positions (p = 0.8952) in trials without a cue.
source: Also, we did not observe a deployment of spatial attention to the fixation target (0.41 ± 0.05) compared with the average across all other positions (p = 0.8952).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data in the no-cue condition.

claim: When the cue was shown shortly before the saccade (50 ms before discrimination target, ~97 ms before saccade), visual sensitivity was higher at the cue (0.78 ± 0.07, p = 0.0002), at the saccade target (0.74 ± 0.07, p < 0.0001) and at the fixation target (0.55 ± 0.05, p = 0.0060), when compared to the average of all tested locations (0.44 ± 0.03).
source: Here, in addition to the fixation and saccade targets, we were also interested in two further locations: the cue location and the retinal location the cue will occupy after the saccade, that is, the remapped location. Visual sensitivity was higher at the cue (0.78 ± 0.07, p = 0.0002), at the saccade target (0.74 ± 0.07, p < 0.0001) and at the fixation target (0.55 ± 0.05, p = 0.0060), when compared to the average of all the tested locations (0.44 ± 0.03).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data in the short-cue condition.

claim: When the cue was shown shortly before the saccade, spatially specific effects were found only at the cue (surround: 0.37 ± 0.03, p < 0.0001) and at the saccade target (surround: 0.40 ± 0.03, p < 0.0001), but not at the fixation target (surround: 0.49 ± 0.03, p = 0.1112).
source: When compared to their closest surrounding positions (Figure 2F), we found spatially specific effects only at the cue (surround: 0.37 ± 0.03, p < 0.0001) and at the saccade target (surround: 0.40 ± 0.03, p < 0.0001), but not at the fixation target (surround: 0.49 ± 0.03, p = 0.1112).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data comparing locations to their surrounds.

claim: When the cue was shown shortly before the saccade, the visual sensitivity at its remapped location (0.46 ± 0.07) was not significantly higher relative to the other tested positions (0.44 ± 0.03, p = 0.6886).
source: Importantly, when the cue was shown shortly before the saccade, the visual sensitivity at its remapped location (0.46 ± 0.07) was not significantly higher relative to the other tested positions (0.44 ± 0.03, p = 0.6886).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data showing no remapping effect in the short-cue condition.

claim: No evidence for attentional remapping of the cued location was observed when the cue appeared shortly before saccade onset.
source: Thus, we observed no evidence for attentional remapping of the cued location when the cue appeared shortly before saccade onset.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the remapped location sensitivity data in the short-cue condition.

claim: When the cue was shown substantially before the discrimination target (200 ms) and on average 240.82 ± 1.42 ms before the saccade onset, higher visual sensitivity was found at the saccade target (0.78 ± 0.08, p = 0.0004), at the cue (0.71 ± 0.06, p < 0.0001) and at the remapped location of the cue (0.56 ± 0.07, p = 0.0072) when compared with the average across all positions (0.45 ± 0.08).
source: Under such conditions, when compared with the average across all positions (0.45 ± 0.08), we found higher visual sensitivity at the saccade target (0.78 ± 0.08, p = 0.0004), at the cue (0.71 ± 0.06, p < 0.0001) and, critically, at the remapped location of the cue (0.56 ± 0.07, p = 0.0072).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data in the long-cue condition.

claim: When the cue was shown substantially before the saccade, the benefits observed at the saccade target (surround: 0.46 ± 0.03, p = 0.0010), at the cue (surround: 0.41 ± 0.04, p < 0.0001) and at its remapped location (surround: 0.45 ± 0.04, p = 0.0382) did not spread towards their respective adjacent positions.
source: Similar to other experimental conditions, the benefits observed at the saccade target (surround: 0.46 ± 0.03, p = 0.0010), at the cue (surround: 0.41 ± 0.04, p < 0.0001) and at its remapped location (surround: 0.45 ± 0.04, p = 0.0382) did not spread towards their respective adjacent positions.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data comparing locations to their surrounds in the long-cue condition.

claim: The increase in sensitivity observed at the remapped location of the cue was present for the condition in which the cue appeared substantially before the discrimination target and the saccade onset, but not if it appeared later.
source: Finally, we found that the increase in sensitivity observed at the remapped location of the cue was present for the condition in which the cue appeared substantially before the discrimination target and the saccade onset, but not if it appeared later.
evidence: This is a comparison finding between the two cue timing conditions.

claim: Normalized sensitivity at the remapped position of the cue in the condition in which no cue was shown (0.38 ± 0.05) was significantly different from conditions in which the cue appeared substantially before the discrimination target and the saccade onset (0.56 ± 0.07, p < 0.0038) but not from conditions in which it appeared later (0.46 ± 0.07, p = 0.2816).
source: Such an effect was evident from comparison of normalized sensitivity obtained at the remapped position of the cue in the condition in which no cue was shown (0.38 ± 0.05) to conditions in which the cue appeared substantially before the discrimination target and the saccade onset (0.56 ± 0.07, p < 0.0038) or to conditions in which it appeared later (0.46 ± 0.07, p = 0.2816).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between conditions.

claim: When the visual system is given enough time to process and attend a visual stimulus, spatial attention is remapped to the retinal location the stimulus will occupy after a saccade.
source: Combined, our results so far show that when the visual system is given enough time to process and attend a visual stimulus, such as the salient cue used in our task, spatial attention is remapped to the retinal location the stimulus will occupy after a saccade.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental findings.

claim: One study reported foveal remapping of the saccade target.
source: Indeed, one study reported such foveal remapping of the saccade target (Rolfs et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study.

claim: Preparation of saccades draws spatial attention away from other, non-saccade or non-salient locations.
source: However, previous research has shown that preparation of saccades draws spatial attention away from other, non-saccade or non-salient locations (Jonikaitis and Theeuwes, 2013), resulting in an increase of acuity threshold in between the fixation and the saccade target locations (Campbell and Wurtz, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the foveal remapping threshold task, the discrimination target had to be tilted by 15.03 ± 2.34° if presented at the fixation target before a saccade.
source: We observed that the discrimination target had to be tilted by 15.03 ± 2.34° if presented at the fixation target before a saccade (Figure 1D), a tilt up to four times bigger than that recorded during the fixation threshold procedure (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a measurement from the foveal remapping threshold task.

claim: In the foveal remapping task, a systematic pre-saccadic deployment of attention towards the saccade target (0.68 ± 0.11, p < 0.0001) was found when compared with the average over all the tested positions (0.36 ± 0.03).
source: Next, and in agreement with the results of the first experiment, we found a systematic pre-saccadic deployment of attention towards the saccade target (Figure 4A, 0.68 ± 0.11, p < 0.0001) when compared with the average over all the tested positions (0.36 ± 0.03).
evidence: This is a finding from the foveal remapping task.

claim: In the foveal remapping task, the pre-saccadic attention benefit was accompanied by systematic deployment of attention at the fixation target (0.96 ± 0.02, p < 0.0001).
source: Critically, this benefit was accompanied by systematic deployment of attention at the fixation target (0.96 ± 0.02, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the foveal remapping task showing foveal remapping.

claim: In the foveal remapping task, the effects at fixation and saccade targets were spatially specific, as shown by significant differences when comparing sensitivity at the fixation target (surround: 0.47 ± 0.06, p < 0.0001) and the saccade target (surround: 0.33 ± 0.04, p < 0.0001) with their relative surrounds.
source: Finally, these effects were spatially specific (Figure 4B), as shown by the significant differences observed when comparing sensitivity at the fixation target (surround: 0.47 ± 0.06, p < 0.0001) and the saccade target (surround: 0.33 ± 0.04, p < 0.0001) with their relative surrounds.
evidence: This is a finding from the foveal remapping task.

claim: Attention consistently shifted to the saccade target location and did not spread to other locations surrounding it.
source: We observed that attention consistently shifted to the saccade target location and, importantly, did not spread to other locations surrounding it.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the spatial attention maps.

claim: A second spatially specific locus of attention was observed at the cued location when a salient cue was presented during saccade preparation.
source: In our main manipulation, we presented a salient cue during saccade preparation. On these trials, we observed a second spatially specific locus of attention at the cued location.
evidence: This is a finding from the cued trials.

claim: A third distinct locus of attention was observed at the retinotopic location the cue would occupy after the saccade.
source: Importantly, on these cued trials, we also observed a third, distinct locus of attention. Although this third location was neither salient, nor task-relevant before the saccade, it corresponded to the retinotopic location the cue would occupy after the saccade.
evidence: This is a finding from the cued trials showing remapping.

claim: Attentional remapping of the cue location before the saccade onset was observed.
source: In other words, we observed attentional remapping of the cue location before the saccade onset.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the observation of attention at the remapped location.

claim: Remapping effects were present only when the cue appeared long enough before the saccade onset.
source: Critically, these effects were present only when the cue appeared long enough before the saccade onset.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the two cue timing conditions.

claim: Remapping, like any other attentional process, requires some time.
source: This indicates that remapping, like any other attentional process, requires some time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the timing-dependent remapping effects.

claim: Three separate foci of attention were observed at the saccade target, cue and remapped location.
source: As we observed three separate foci of attention (at the saccade target, cue and remapped location), we did not find support for the hypothesis that attention spreads during saccade preparation around the saccade target (Zirnsak and Moore, 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of the spatial attention findings.

claim: No support was found for the hypothesis that attention spreads during saccade preparation around the saccade target.
source: As we observed three separate foci of attention (at the saccade target, cue and remapped location), we did not find support for the hypothesis that attention spreads during saccade preparation around the saccade target (Zirnsak and Moore, 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial specificity of attention findings, contrasting with the convergent remapping hypothesis.

claim: The link between behavioral effects and neurophysiology is only theoretical.
source: As we report behavioral results, it is important to note that the link between our effects and neurophysiology is only theoretical.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of behavioral studies.

claim: Behavioral experiments do not allow for direct conclusions as to which neural structures are involved in remapping nor on the validity of neurophysiology findings.
source: Behavioral experiments do not allow for direct conclusions as to which neural structures are involved in remapping nor on the validity of neurophysiology findings.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of behavioral studies.

claim: The findings are relevant to the behavioral predictions provided in earlier neurophysiology work.
source: However, our findings are relevant to the behavioural predictions provided in earlier neurophysiology work.
evidence: This is a statement about the relevance of the current findings to previous work.

claim: Combined behavioral and neuronal recordings are necessary to eventually link proposals of neuronal activity before saccades and behavioral observations.
source: Combined behavioral and neuronal recordings are necessary to eventually link proposals of neuronal activity before saccades and behavioral observations reported here and previously.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Forward remapping offers an excellent candidate mechanism of space constancy.
source: This so-called forward remapping offers an excellent candidate mechanism of space constancy that has been incorporated into such phenomenon models.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical importance of forward remapping.

claim: In forward remapping models, connections between visual neurons with receptive fields spatially separated by the saccade vector can be used to predict post-saccadic visual stimulus location and compensate for retinal image shifts during the saccade.
source: In these models, connections between visual neurons with receptive fields spatially separated by the saccade vector can be used to predict post-saccadic visual stimulus location and compensate for retinal image shifts during the saccade (Neupane et al., 2017; Quaia et al., 1998; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of forward remapping models from the literature.

claim: Zirnsak and colleagues' results suggested that early findings on forward remapping were affected by the low spatial resolution of the receptive field mapping technique.
source: However, forward remapping models have been challenged by Zirnsak and colleagues (Chen et al., 2018; Zirnsak et al., 2014), whose results suggested that the early findings were affected by the low spatial resolution of the receptive field mapping technique (Duhamel et al., 1992; Sommer and Wurtz, 2006; Walker et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a summary of the critique from Zirnsak and colleagues.

claim: More detailed FEF receptive field mapping suggested that, before a saccade, cells preferentially respond to stimuli presented near the saccade target rather than at the remapped target location.
source: More detailed FEF receptive field mapping suggested that, before a saccade, cells preferentially respond to stimuli presented near the saccade target rather than at the remapped target location.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Zirnsak and colleagues.

claim: Cell receptive fields do not shift in parallel to the saccade vector, but instead converge towards the saccade target.
source: In other words, cell receptive fields do not shift in parallel to the saccade vector, but instead converge towards the saccade target.
evidence: This is a summary of the convergent remapping findings.

claim: Zirnsak and colleagues argued that forward remapping models cannot explain space constancy and instead one should focus on saccade target selection as a mechanism mediating this phenomenon.
source: Zirnsak and colleagues thus argued that forward remapping models cannot explain space constancy and instead one should focus on saccade target selection as a mechanism mediating this phenomenon (Zirnsak and Moore, 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of the argument from Zirnsak and Moore, 2014.

claim: The visual system may implement both forward and convergent remapping of receptive fields in area V4.
source: More recent work has indicated that the visual system may, in fact, implement both forward and convergent remapping of receptive fields in area V4 (Neupane et al., 2016b; Neupane et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Neupane et al., 2016a and 2016b.

claim: The combined approach of forward and convergent remapping has been criticized on technical grounds.
source: As this combined approach has been criticized on technical grounds (Hartmann et al., 2017), the neurophysiological results regarding the existence of forward remapping remain inconclusive.
evidence: This is a summary of criticism from Hartmann et al., 2017.

claim: The neurophysiological results regarding the existence of forward remapping remain inconclusive.
source: As this combined approach has been criticized on technical grounds (Hartmann et al., 2017), the neurophysiological results regarding the existence of forward remapping remain inconclusive.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of neurophysiological evidence.

claim: A number of behavioral studies have repeatedly and reliably demonstrated forward remapping of spatial attention before saccades.
source: On the other hand, a number of behavioral studies have repeatedly and reliably demonstrated forward remapping of spatial attention before saccades (Jonikaitis et al., 2013; Rolfs et al., 2011; Szinte et al., 2015; Szinte et al., 2016; Yao et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is a summary of behavioral evidence from multiple studies.

claim: Previous behavioral studies suffered from low spatial resolution, similar to early neurophysiological studies.
source: The behavioral studies, however, suffered from the same drawbacks as early neurophysiological studies, low spatial resolution.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of limitations in previous behavioral work.

claim: The current study has eliminated the potential criticism of low spatial resolution.
source: Our study has eliminated this potential criticism, and our observed deployment of attention in the opposite direction of the saccade and of the cue speaks in favor of the forward remapping effects.
evidence: This is a claim about the methodological improvement of the current study.

claim: The observed deployment of attention in the opposite direction of the saccade and of the cue speaks in favor of the forward remapping effects.
source: Our study has eliminated this potential criticism, and our observed deployment of attention in the opposite direction of the saccade and of the cue speaks in favor of the forward remapping effects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to forward remapping.

claim: Spatial attention is allocated to the saccade target and does not broadly spread around it.
source: Consistent with previous behavioral studies (Baldauf and Deubel, 2008; Deubel and Schneider, 1996; Jonikaitis et al., 2017) and contrary to the convergent remapping effects, our results show that spatial attention is allocated to the saccade target and does not broadly spread around it.
evidence: This is a finding consistent with previous behavioral studies and contrary to convergent remapping predictions.

claim: Convergent remapping cannot account for a number of earlier behavioral findings.
source: Additionally, convergent remapping cannot account for a number of earlier behavioral findings (Jonikaitis et al., 2013; Rolfs et al., 2011; Szinte et al., 2015; Szinte et al., 2016), as such spread of attention would have to be asymmetric and not spread towards the several control positions tested in these earlier studies.
evidence: This is an argument based on the incompatibility of convergent remapping with previous findings.

claim: Increasing the neural spatial sampling at a particular position results in reduction of spatial uncertainty.
source: Perhaps counterintuitively, recent computational neuroimaging modeling (Kay et al., 2015) has shown that increasing the neural spatial sampling at a particular position, similar to over-sampling of the saccade target observed within convergent remapping studies (Hartmann et al., 2017; Tolias et al., 2001; Zirnsak et al., 2014), results in reduction of spatial uncertainty.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling cited from Kay et al., 2015.

claim: Convergent remapping does not necessarily yield a large spread of attention around the saccade goal.
source: Convergent remapping does not necessarily yield a large spread of attention around the saccade goal (Zirnsak and Moore, 2014).
evidence: This is a reinterpretation of convergent remapping based on computational modeling insights.

claim: Convergent remapping may increase visual sensitivity to stimuli only in the immediate vicinity of the saccade target.
source: Rather, it may increase visual sensitivity to stimuli only in the immediate vicinity of the saccade target.
evidence: This is a reinterpretation of what convergent remapping might mean behaviorally.

claim: Convergent remapping could reflect the spatially specific attentional selection of the saccade target observed in the present study.
source: Convergent remapping could, therefore, reflect the spatially specific attentional selection of the saccade target observed in the present study.
evidence: This is a proposed reconciliation of convergent remapping with the current findings.

claim: Spatial visual attention mechanisms must be accounted for in future work of remapping to advance our understanding of space constancy.
source: Our results indicate that spatial visual attention mechanisms must be accounted for in future work of remapping to advance our understanding of space constancy.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the current findings.

claim: Previous reports of convergent remapping may reflect increased visual sensitivity at the saccade target explained by both spatial and temporal properties of visual attention.
source: Here, we hypothesize that previous reports of convergent remapping may reflect increased visual sensitivity at the saccade target explained by both spatial and temporal properties of visual attention.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to reconcile convergent remapping findings with attention mechanisms.

claim: Localized visual probes used to determine visual neuron RF spatial profile are likely to capture spatial attention.
source: First, to determine a visual neuron RF spatial profile, neurophysiologists used localized visual probes, presented most of the time in a sparse display with high probe-background contrast. It is, therefore, likely that such probes capture spatial attention (Theeuwes, 1991).
evidence: This is an inference about methodological issues in neurophysiology studies, supported by citation.

claim: Visual RFs can shift towards attended locations even without any saccade involved.
source: As visual RFs can shift towards attended locations even without any saccade involved (Niebergall et al., 2011; Womelsdorf et al., 2006), one must account for the effect of attention before interpreting any RF change in spatial tuning.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Niebergall et al., 2011 and Womelsdorf et al., 2006.

claim: One must account for the effect of attention before interpreting any RF change in spatial tuning.
source: As visual RFs can shift towards attended locations even without any saccade involved (Niebergall et al., 2011; Womelsdorf et al., 2006), one must account for the effect of attention before interpreting any RF change in spatial tuning.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the interaction between attention and RF properties.

claim: To understand pre-saccadic RF changes in spatial tuning, one should first consider the spatial deployment of spatial attention.
source: To understand pre-saccadic RF changes in spatial tuning, one should first consider the spatial deployment of spatial attention.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the current findings.

claim: The temporal dynamics of attention have to be accounted for to understand pre-saccadic RF changes.
source: Second, we argue that the temporal dynamics of attention have to be accounted for.
evidence: This is an argument based on the timing-dependent effects observed in the study.

claim: The time at which the cue was presented was critical for remapping of attention to be observed before the saccade.
source: We found that the time at which we presented our cue was critical for remapping of attention to be observed before the saccade.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental manipulation of cue timing.

claim: Benefits at the remapped location of the cue were observed only when the cue was shown more than 175 ms before the saccade onset.
source: In particular, benefits at the remapped location of the cue were observed only when the cue was shown more than 175 ms before the saccade onset.
evidence: This is a specific finding about the timing threshold for remapping.

claim: The fastest deployment of attention would take a minimum of 100 ms to occur.
source: As even the fastest deployment of attention would take a minimum of 100 ms to occur (Ling and Carrasco, 2006; Müller and Rabbitt, 1989; Nakayama and Mackeben, 1989; Rolfs and Carrasco, 2012), our remapping effects are compatible with the time course of attentional selection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about attention dynamics from cited literature.

claim: The remapping effects are compatible with the time course of attentional selection.
source: As even the fastest deployment of attention would take a minimum of 100 ms to occur (Ling and Carrasco, 2006; Müller and Rabbitt, 1989; Nakayama and Mackeben, 1989; Rolfs and Carrasco, 2012), our remapping effects are compatible with the time course of attentional selection.
evidence: This is an interpretation relating the timing findings to attention dynamics.

claim: A fair proportion of visual neurons recorded within LIP and earlier visual areas showed forward remapping activity for probes presented as early as 250 ms before the saccade.
source: In particular, it was reported that a fair proportion of visual neurons recorded within LIP (Kusunoki and Goldberg, 2003) and earlier visual areas (Nakamura and Colby, 2002) showed forward remapping activity for probes presented as early as 250 ms before the saccade.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Kusunoki and Goldberg, 2003 and Nakamura and Colby, 2002.

claim: Forward remapping activity preceding the saccade onset was observed only if a visual object was flashed early before the saccade.
source: Interestingly, they observed forward remapping activity preceding the saccade onset only if a visual object was flashed early before the saccade, such that visual objects shown earlier relative to the eye movement resulted in delayed activity during or after the saccade onset (Kusunoki and Goldberg, 2003; Nakamura and Colby, 2002).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Kusunoki and Goldberg, 2003 and Nakamura and Colby, 2002.

claim: The current results are consistent with findings from Kusunoki and Goldberg, 2003 and Nakamura and Colby, 2002.
source: Our results are consistent with these findings, but not with those of Wang and colleagues (Wang et al., 2016), which report that the presentation of a visual object before the saccade resulted only in post-saccadic forward remapping activities within a set of recorded cells in LIP.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with previous neurophysiology studies.

claim: Wang and colleagues reported that the presentation of a visual object before the saccade resulted only in post-saccadic forward remapping activities within a set of recorded cells in LIP.
source: Our results are consistent with these findings, but not with those of Wang and colleagues (Wang et al., 2016), which report that the presentation of a visual object before the saccade resulted only in post-saccadic forward remapping activities within a set of recorded cells in LIP.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Wang et al., 2016.

claim: Wang and colleagues found that the recorded cells responded transiently to the intermediate position between the current and the future receptive field position.
source: Moreover, they found that the recorded cells responded transiently to the intermediate position between the current and the future receptive field position.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Wang et al., 2016.

claim: No benefit was observed at locations between the cue and the remapped position of the cue in the current study.
source: By contrast, we did not observe any benefit at locations between the cue and the remapped position of the cue.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study that contrasts with Wang et al., 2016.

claim: Remapping of attention better reflects the activity of early visual areas than attentional priority maps (LIP, FEF, SC).
source: These effects suggest that remapping of attention better reflects the activity of early visual areas than attentional priority maps (LIP, FEF, SC).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pattern of findings in relation to different brain areas.

claim: Neurophysiology studies that failed to observe pre-saccadic forward remapping typically presented probes shortly before (50 ms) the saccade.
source: It is important to note that neurophysiology studies that failed to observe pre-saccadic forward remapping typically presented probes shortly before (50 ms) the saccade.
evidence: This is an observation about methodological patterns in neurophysiology studies.

claim: A short time window between probe presentation and neural recording might be insufficient for probes to be remapped to a location parallel to the saccade before the onset of the movement.
source: Our behavioral findings suggest that a short time window between probe presentation and neural recording, which some studies have used, might be insufficient for probes to be remapped to a location parallel to the saccade before the onset of the movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in relation to neurophysiology methodology.

claim: For attended stimuli shown just prior to the saccade onset, remapping may occur during or after the saccade.
source: Further, if remapping is closely related to the time course of attention, it is possible that for attended stimuli shown just prior to the saccade onset, remapping may occur during or after the saccade (Kusunoki and Goldberg, 2003; Nakamura and Colby, 2002).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the timing findings and cited literature.

claim: Neupane and colleagues observed forward remapping when measuring post-saccadic memory responses to probes shown just before the saccade.
source: Indeed, Neupane and colleagues (Neupane et al., 2016a; Neupane et al., 2016b) observed forward remapping when measuring post-saccadic memory responses to probes shown just before the saccade.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Neupane et al., 2016a and 2016b.

claim: A post-saccadic memory trace of remapping was enhanced by attentional modulations established before the saccade.
source: Also, Yao and colleagues (Yao et al., 2016a) have shown that a post-saccadic memory trace of remapping was enhanced by attentional modulations established before the saccade, corroborating the notion that forward remapping can occur after the saccade.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Yao et al., 2016a.

claim: Forward remapping can occur after the saccade.
source: Also, Yao and colleagues (Yao et al., 2016a) have shown that a post-saccadic memory trace of remapping was enhanced by attentional modulations established before the saccade, corroborating the notion that forward remapping can occur after the saccade.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by citation to Yao et al., 2016a.

claim: Two previous studies found that spatial attention was allocated to the location of a salient stimulus immediately after the saccade, even when the stimulus was no longer present.
source: Both studies found that spatial attention was allocated to the location of a salient stimulus immediately after the saccade, even when the stimulus was no longer present (Jonikaitis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous behavioral studies.

claim: The visual system anticipates the attended stimulus location after a saccade and recomputes its retinotopic location before the saccade is done.
source: This indicates that the visual system anticipates the attended stimulus location after a saccade and recomputes its retinotopic location before the saccade is done.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the post-saccadic attention findings.

claim: High perceptual performance was observed at fixation in the current study.
source: Finally, we also observed high perceptual performance at fixation, a result in line with two previous studies that investigated foveal remapping effects (Knapen et al., 2016; Rolfs et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from the foveal remapping task.

claim: The high perceptual performance at fixation is in line with two previous studies that investigated foveal remapping effects.
source: Finally, we also observed high perceptual performance at fixation, a result in line with two previous studies that investigated foveal remapping effects (Knapen et al., 2016; Rolfs et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies.

claim: One would expect that visual selection should prioritize the saccade target, whereas the current fixation should be the least informative and least attended part of the display.
source: Such an attentional effect is surprising, as one would expect that visual selection should prioritize the saccade target, whereas the current fixation should be the least informative and least attended part of the display (especially given that participants already fixated for ~1 s before starting saccade preparation).
evidence: This is a statement about expected attention allocation based on task relevance.

claim: If one considers that fixation-centered receptive fields will process the saccade target after the saccade, forward remapping effects suggest significant attentional benefits at that location.
source: However, if one considers that fixation-centered receptive fields will process the saccade target after the saccade, forward remapping effects suggest significant attentional benefits at that location, as we observed here and in a previous study (Rolfs et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an explanation for the surprising fixation effect based on forward remapping logic.

claim: Marino and Mazer recently showed that attention modulates the state of neurons in V4 before saccade onset, without a substantial shift of neurons' spatial tuning.
source: Marino and Mazer (Marino and Mazer, 2018) recently showed that attention modulates the state of neurons in V4 before saccade onset, without a substantial shift of neurons' spatial tuning.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Marino and Mazer, 2018.

claim: Marino and Mazer used a sustained attention task to a cue presented before a series of records, in contrast to the current study which manipulated transient attention by cueing a location on every trial.
source: In contrast to our study, which manipulated transient attention by cueing a location on every trial, they used a sustained attention task to a cue presented before a series of records.
evidence: This is a comparison of methodological differences between studies.

claim: Marino and Mazer's pre-saccadic effects are consistent with the results reported in the current study.
source: Their pre-saccadic effects are consistent with the results reported here and suggest that new models of space constancy should account for the dynamics of spatial attention.
evidence: This is a comparison showing consistency between studies.

claim: New models of space constancy should account for the dynamics of spatial attention.
source: Their pre-saccadic effects are consistent with the results reported here and suggest that new models of space constancy should account for the dynamics of spatial attention.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future modeling work based on the current and related findings.

claim: An eccentricity-adjusted discrimination task was used to measure spatial attention maps before saccades for the first time.
source: In summary, we used an eccentricity-adjusted discrimination task to measure, for the first time, spatial attention maps before saccades.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the methodological approach.

claim: A spatially specific increase in visual sensitivity was observed at the fixation target, the saccade target, the cue and the remapped location of the cue.
source: Using this method, we observed a spatially specific increase in visual sensitivity at the fixation target, the saccade target, the cue and the remapped location of the cue.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Before a saccade, attention is deployed towards the saccade target as well as towards a cued location.
source: We found that, before a saccade, attention is deployed towards the saccade target as well as towards a cued location.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about attention deployment.

claim: Given that the cue was presented sufficiently early before the saccade, a deployment of attention to its remapped location was observed, that is parallel and opposite to the saccade vector.
source: Further, given that the cue was presented sufficiently early before the saccade, we observed a deployment of attention to its remapped location, that is parallel and opposite to the saccade vector.
evidence: This is a summary of the main remapping finding.

claim: The benefit at the remapped location is smaller compared with that at the cue location.
source: Although the benefit at that location is smaller compared with that at the cue location, it reflects an ongoing process that facilitates spatial attention allocation after the saccade despite the retinotopic shifts induced by the eye movement.
evidence: This is an observation about the magnitude of the remapping effect.

claim: The benefit at the remapped location reflects an ongoing process that facilitates spatial attention allocation after the saccade despite the retinotopic shifts induced by the eye movement.
source: Although the benefit at that location is smaller compared with that at the cue location, it reflects an ongoing process that facilitates spatial attention allocation after the saccade despite the retinotopic shifts induced by the eye movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the remapping effect.

claim: Eighteen students participated in the experiment.
source: Eighteen students (14 participants in the peripheral remapping task, eight participants in the foveal remapping task, four participants did both tasks) of the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitä München participated in the experiment (ages 22–30, 10 female, one author), for a compensation of 10 Euros per hour of testing.
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: All participants except the author were naive as to the purpose of the study.
source: All participants except the author were naive as to the purpose of the study and all had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: This is a description of participant characteristics.

claim: The experiments were undertaken with the understanding and written informed consent of all participants.
source: The experiments were undertaken with the understanding and written informed consent of all participants and were carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical procedures.

claim: Participants completed between 2914 and 3323 trials of the peripheral remapping task.
source: Participants completed between 2914 and 3323 trials of the peripheral remapping task.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: On average, 25.38 ± 0.76 trials and 16.13 ± 0.42 trials per participant were analyzed at the frequently and less frequently tested positions, respectively, in each of the three main conditions.
source: On average, we analyzed 25.38 ± 0.76 trials and 16.13 ± 0.42 trials per participant at the frequently and less frequently tested positions, respectively, in each of the three main conditions.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis sample size.

claim: In total, 36,236 trials (90.41% of the online accepted trials, 82.20% of all trials) were included in the peripheral remapping main task.
source: In total, we included 36,236 trials (90.41% of the online accepted trials, 82.20% of all trials) in the peripheral remapping main task and 7306 trials (95.13% of the online accepted trials, 86.85% of all trials) of the foveal remapping main task.
evidence: This is a description of the final analyzed sample.

claim: 7306 trials (95.13% of the online accepted trials, 86.85% of all trials) were included in the foveal remapping main task.
source: In total, we included 36,236 trials (90.41% of the online accepted trials, 82.20% of all trials) in the peripheral remapping main task and 7306 trials (95.13% of the online accepted trials, 86.85% of all trials) of the foveal remapping main task.
evidence: This is a description of the final analyzed sample.
